prize_parts.citation: For the discovery of halide perovskites as high-efficiency solution-processed solar-cell absorbers

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize for halide perovskite absorbers to Miyasaka, Snaith and Park. The ABX3 family gives a clean structure-to-function story: composition, cation and halide mixing and defect chemistry set absorption, carrier lifetime and band gap, and the principle that a defect-tolerant, solution-processed semiconductor can be a high-efficiency absorber has been independently reproduced for over a decade. Round 1 did not weaken the science. It moved the debate to citation wording and attribution, and those I can answer. The citation should name the absorber material and its demonstrated efficiency, not deployment, modules or lifetimes. That keeps the open stability and lead questions outside what is being credited, and the same logic is how earlier prizes treated discoveries whose engineering was still ongoing.
statement.case_against: Operational stability and lead toxicity remain unresolved, and early efficiency claims were affected by hysteresis in current-voltage measurements, so a sceptic can say that the device story is not fully clean. Six names are credited, and any trio omits Gratzel, Kanatzidis or Seok. Round 1 also left perovskites with only two explicit supporters, no better than B054 or B069, so I cannot claim a majority and I do not treat support counts as the argument. If the committee decides a prize needs deployment-scale evidence, this candidate is weaker than I have argued.

responses.point: Linke asks that the citation rest on the absorber and efficiency rather than deployment, and asks whether Kanatzidis or Gratzel should displace Park in the trio.
responses.response: I agree on the citation. On the trio I would keep Park. Miyasaka made the first perovskite-sensitized cell in 2009 and Park's 2011 and 2012 work and the solid-state devices of Park and of Snaith with Miyasaka's group are what turned the material into a thin-film absorber of real efficiency. Gratzel's solid-state cell and Kanatzidis's work on lead-free and tin halide structures and on composition are important but are developments or parallel lines more than the origin of the absorber result. I would rather admit the cut is contestable than add a fourth name, which the rules do not permit.

responses.point: Brzezinski doubts that perovskites are better defined than degraders: six plausible names, hysteresis artefacts in early efficiency records, and stability that bears on maturity.
responses.response: The hysteresis point is fair, and I would use it to set the evidence standard: credit only what stabilised-power-output and certified measurements support. Those exist, and the independent reproduction does not depend on the earliest numbers, so the absorber discovery and the device engineering can be separated, as you ask. I do not think the attribution is cleaner for B054 where you yourself list eight names and two lineages. I accept your point that stability weighs on maturity, but I put it on the application, not on whether the principle was discovered and verified.

responses.point: Chabes pairs base editing (Liu) with heterobifunctional degraders (Crews, Deshaies) as a two-part chemical-control-of-biology prize with three names in total.
responses.response: The pairing is coherent as a theme, and I take the point that it keeps the credit to three people. My hesitation is that both parts are medicine-facing and neither has a drug approved on the mechanism cited, so the maturity test is applied more loosely than it is to perovskites, where the principle has been verified in thousands of independent devices. I also think leaving Handa and Ito out of the degrader citation, and Komor and Gaudelli out of base editing, costs more credit than my cut for B017 does.

responses.point: Sparr asks whether the committee should reward a device-efficiency breakthrough while stability is unproven, or a concept like phase separation tested for longer in many systems.
responses.response: I would frame it as a materials discovery and not a device record. The tested claim is that these halides are strong, defect-tolerant absorbers, verified by structural, spectroscopic and device studies in many groups. Phase separation has been argued longer, but the chair's summary shows the in vivo question is still open, which is a maturity problem of a different kind from a stability problem in a verified material. I do not move to B044, though I understand why you would ask.

uncertainties: Whether colleagues will accept a Miyasaka, Snaith and Park cut that leaves out Gratzel, Kanatzidis and Seok.
Whether stability, lead toxicity and early hysteresis artefacts weigh enough with others to make perovskites look premature, and whether the citation can be worded to avoid that.
Whether B054 can reach a majority once its scope (PROTAC design or cereblon mechanism) and laureates are settled, in which case I would consider it as my fallback.
For nitrogenase (B062), whether a structure-led citation is acceptable while the catalytic mechanism is unsettled.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict or recusal need for any shortlisted candidate. I work on electron crystallography and framework materials, which is adjacent to perovskite and nitrogenase structural questions but involves no personal or institutional tie to any credited person. Peter Brzezinski is a Stockholm University colleague, which is not a conflict for any shortlisted candidate. Unchanged from round 1.
